introduction: At the advanced level, examiners heavily test permutations, probability thresholds, and the mental manipulation of 3D objects—skills highly crucial for spatial reasoning in engineering.

core_concepts.title: Permutation vs. Combination
core_concepts.description:
1. **Permutation ($^nP_r$):** Used when the **Order or Arrangement** strictly matters (e.g., generating a password, seating people in chairs).
2. **Combination ($^nC_r$):** Used when ONLY the **Selection** matters, and order is completely irrelevant (e.g., forming a project team, drawing cards from a deck).

core_concepts.title: Probability Fundamentals
core_concepts.description:
Basic Formula: $P(E) = \frac{\text{Favorable Outcomes}}{\text{Total Possible Outcomes}}$.
- **Mutually Exclusive Events:** Cannot happen simultaneously. Rule: $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$.
- **Independent Events:** The occurrence of one has absolutely zero effect on the other. Rule: $P(A \cap B) = P(A) \times P(B)$.

core_concepts.title: Spatial Aptitude
core_concepts.description:
Recently heavily emphasized in GATE. Involves the mental manipulation of 2D and 3D geometric shapes:
1. **Paper Folding & Cutting:** Always start from the absolute final cut and unfold backward. Unfolding acts exactly like drawing a 'Mirror Image' across the fold line.
2. **Dice Reasoning:** In a 'Standard Dice', the sum of the numbers on strictly opposite faces is always exactly 7.

important_entities.name: The AND/OR Rule
important_entities.significance: A golden rule in P&C and Probability: Whenever you use the word 'AND' logically, you must mathematically **Multiply ($\times$)**. Whenever you use the word 'OR' logically, you must mathematically **Add ($+$)**.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation:
Advanced Exam Trap: Calculating the probability of 'at least one' by adding up multiple individual cases (1, 2, 3...) wastes massive amounts of exam time. 
The ultimate shortcut: **$P(\text{At least one}) = 1 - P(\text{None})$**.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: In calendar problems, dividing any number of days by 7 gives the weeks. The absolute remainder is called the 'Odd Days'. A standard year has exactly 1 Odd Day; a Leap Year has exactly 2 Odd Days.

exam_strategy_tips: A favorite GATE and UPSC numerical trap: 'If 5 people sit around a circular table, how many distinct arrangements are possible?' Answer: Circular permutations strictly follow $(n-1)!$. Therefore, $4! = 24$ ways.
